### Site and method
EBTL is a ~70-acre dry-deciduous restoration site in the Krishnagiri Eastern Ghats foothills, near **Chinnathamandrapalli / Veppanapalli** (~724 m), described by the project as degraded valley forest with remnant wildlife ([ebtl.earth](https://ebtl.earth/)).

I treated “occur inside EBTL” as **resident or regular use of that parcel**, then checked:
1. published range / taxonomy  
2. local herpetofauna surveys  
3. nearby comparable sanctuaries  
4. occurrence databases (GBIF / iNaturalist)  
5. habitat fit for a large snake-eating elapid  

### What the regional evidence shows

| Evidence | Finding | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| **Local surveys** | Ganesh et al. (2018) surveyed Melagiri–Bilgiri–Arcot massifs (incl. Melagiri / Hosur area). Elapids found: *Calliophis melanurus*, *Bungarus caeruleus*, *Naja naja* — **no *Ophiophagus*** ([AJCB PDF](http://www.ajcb.in/journals/full_papers_july_2018/AJCB-Vol7-No1-Ganesh%20et%20al.pdf)). | High |
| **Hosur / Melagiri fauna** | ANCF vertebrate inventory lists spectacled cobra & krait, **not king cobra** ([ancf_melagiris.pdf](http://kans.org.in/sites/default/files/ancf_melagiris.pdf)); Melagiri reptile summaries match that ([Wikipedia: Melagiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melagiri)). | High |
| **Nearest similar habitat** | Koundinya WLS (~60 km; dry deciduous, elephants) lists common cobra/python, **not king cobra** ([AP Forest Dept](https://forests.ap.gov.in/kaundinya.php)). | Medium–high |
| **Occurrence data** | GBIF: **0** *Ophiophagus* records in ~11–14°N, 77–80°E. Nearest wild-looking GBIF points are **~250 km** away in the Western Ghats. iNaturalist hits near Bannerghatta (~67 km) are **captive**. | High |
| **Confirmed Eastern Ghats populations** | Active EG records are mainly **north coastal Andhra / Papikonda** (~600+ km), not southern dry EG Tamil Nadu ([EGWS](https://eghats.org/program/king-cobra-conservation); Balaji & Satyanarayana 2018). | High |
| **Western Ghats species** | *Ophiophagus kaalinga* is **Western Ghats–endemic**; nearest TN rescues are Coimbatore / Nilgiri foothills (~200 km) ([EJT revision](https://europeanjournaloftaxonomy.eu/index.php/ejt/article/view/2681); Coimbatore rescue reports). | High |
| **Habitat at EBTL** | Small, degraded dry-deciduous patch; king cobras need large ranges and high snake prey density. Wikipedia/range texts that say “Eastern Ghats … Tamil Nadu” are **coarse** and not backed by Krishnagiri vouchers. | Medium |

**Best estimate:** roughly **<10%** chance of regular occurrence on the EBTL parcel; **<5%** for a resident/breeding presence. Transient wanderers can’t be ruled out at very low probability, but local absence across multiple surveys makes that a thin tail.

### What would make me trust or reject this

**Would strengthen / confirm the “unlikely” call**
- Continued lack of verified IDs in Krishnagiri / Melagiri / Hosur rescues and surveys  
- No camera-trap or expert-vouchered records within ~50–100 km  
- EBTL remains a small, open, regenerating dry patch without dense contiguous forest  

**Would force me to revise upward (reject the low estimate)**
- A **photo-vouchered** wild king cobra from EBTL, Veppanapalli, Melagiri, or Koundinya, ID’d by a competent herpetologist  
- Forest Department rescue with unambiguous *Ophiophagus* ID in Krishnagiri/Hosur  
- Repeated independent sightings, nest, or roadkill with locality data  
- New systematic survey detecting the species in Cauvery North / Melagiri  

**Caveats:** absence of evidence isn’t proof of absolute absence; surveys miss rare snakes. Still, for this landscape the negative evidence is consistent across surveys, news, databases, and nearest analogous forests — so “likely to occur inside EBTL” is not supported.

Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) - A forest restoration project in the Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu

Over decades, the dry deciduous forests of our country have been stripped and exploited for commercial use. As native forests receded to only higher elevations of hills, creatures of the forests have also lost their footing in the valley. EBTL lies in one of those valleys. In the foothills of a degraded forest.

These 70 acres now 'belong' to us. How wonderful would it be if the other creatures also echoed the same thought? Our goal is to help the forest regain its rich biodiversity.

The year we began work, a few elephants came to the land, something that had never happened in the last many decades. We decided to call this project.

# Elephants By The Lake!

# The map of EBTL

Once you step into the hills around EBTL there are remnants of a once thriving forest; bird calls, fresh bear tracks, the jumping away of a troupe of langurs, trees in bloom or seed, spiders waiting for a catch, the scuffling across of a monitor lizard, a bird of prey gliding above.

Unfortunately this biodiverse ecosystem of the Eastern Ghats has been almost eradicated in terms of its area, but for a few hilly pockets where the tough terrain has made it too difficult for people to interfere.

Hopefully in time, the land will begin a cycle of regeneration where at a point, this space can become a safe corner for some of the rarer and threatened flora of the Eastern Ghats to flourish and wildlife can reinhabit the land.

# What happens at EBTL

#### Forest restoration

EBTL, primarily is focused on the native flora of the dry decidious forests of the South Deccan plateau.

#### Centre for Eastern Ghats Studies

## Our Programs

## King Cobra Conservation

The King Cobra is listed under the Schedule-II of the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and catergorized as "Vulnerable" in the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Once believed to be locally extinct in North Coastal Andhra Pradesh (Eastern Ghats), our team had been documenting consistent reports of kills from across the region since 2008. The Eastern Ghats are discontinuous range of mountains with predominantly moist deciduous and thorny scrub habitats. A unique habitat compared to known wetter habitats of king cobras. Using an open responsive framework, we aim to study the ecology of king cobras of the Eastern Ghats.

Being an apex predator, king cobras are indicative of the health of herpetofauna of the region. We pioneered a unique "Snake Savior" Program wherein we train select community members in not only rescuing any king cobras from human habitations but also conserve the breeeding habitat of the species by working with the Andhra Pradesh Forest Department and other stakeholders.

For the first time in the conservation history of the eastern ghats region, we have been successfully rescuing king cobras from human-dominated landscapes through our snake saviors stationed across the region and also protected a king cobra nest for the very first time in the region with help from the local community.

    d = q(f"scientificName=Ophiophagus&country=IN&hasCoordinate=true&limit=100&offset={offset}")

    if offset >= d['count']:
        break

import math
def hav(a,b):
    R=6371
    lat1,lon1=map(math.radians,a)
    lat2,lon2=map(math.radians,b)

    h=math.sin(dlat/2)**2+math.cos(lat1)*math.cos(lat2)*math.sin(dlon/2)**2
    return 2*R*math.asin(math.sqrt(h))

near = sorted([(hav(ebtl,(lat,lon)), lat, lon, y, s, loc) for lat,lon,y,s,loc in allp])[:15]
print(f"Total IN coord records fetched: {len(allp)}")

Synthesis:
Kaundinya Wildlife Sanctuary is an elephant reserve located in the Chittoor district of Andhra Pradesh [1][2]. While the sanctuary is home to many reptiles including the common cobra and Indian rock python [1][3], king cobras are not typically cited as a primary inhabitant of this specific area [1][4]. King cobra conservation efforts in Andhra Pradesh are primarily focused on the Eastern Ghats and areas like Papikonda National Park, rather than the Chittoor or Tirupati regions [5][6][7]. An elephant corridor is planned to connect Kaundinya with the Seshachalam-based Sri Venkateswara National Park [2][4].

Site description: Kaundinya Wildlife Sanctuary covers an area of 35,760 ha in Kuppam and Palmaner Ranges of Chittoor district, Andhra Pradesh. It is the only Sanctuary in Andhra Pradesh known for harbouring a population of Asian elephants, which reportedly reappeared in 1984 after 200 years (Prasad and Reddy 2002). The Sanctuary has Dry Deciduous forests, with thorny scrub interspersed with trees providing a good habitat for Asian Elephants. These forests have small ponds, tanks and the Kaundinya and Kaigal tributaries of Palar River, which provide the main sources of water for the animals. The Sanctuary is situated 50 km from Chittoor and 120 km from Bangalore.

Summary of threats to biodiversity at KBA: MAIN THREATS: Man-animal conflict; Over-grazing; Illegal wood collection. Since the Asian Elephants reappeared in Kaundinya WLS, it has become the focus of conservation action. Seven villages are situated inside the Sanctuary. Insufficient fodder in the forest due to severe over-grazing by livestock, and the availability of crops such as sugarcane, sorghum and ragi attract elephants to them, resulting in man-animal conflict. Sadly, till 2002, 42 people have been killed by elephants (Prasad and Reddy 2002). At the same time, 12 elephants were electrocuted to death by the angry villagers. Kalyani dam in Chamala Valley near Thirupathi is found to be a good habitat for elephants. The Chamala Valley is included in Sri Venkateswara National Park (also an IBA). A corridor for elephants is planned between Koundinya and Sri Venkateswara under Project Elephant (Prasad and Reddy 2002). With better habitat protection under Project Elephant, the Yellow-throated Bulbul would also benefit, along with other dry land bird species.</content>

<content>Eastern Ghats Wildlife Society

## Our Programs

## King Cobra Conservation

The King Cobra is listed under the Schedule-II of the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and catergorized as "Vulnerable" in the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Once believed to be locally extinct in North Coastal Andhra Pradesh (Eastern Ghats), our team had been documenting consistent reports of kills from across the region since 2008. The Eastern Ghats are discontinuous range of mountains with predominantly moist deciduous and thorny scrub habitats. A unique habitat compared to known wetter habitats of king cobras. Using an open responsive framework, we aim to study the ecology of king cobras of the Eastern Ghats.

Being an apex predator, king cobras are indicative of the health of herpetofauna of the region. We pioneered a unique "Snake Savior" Program wherein we train select community members in not only rescuing any king cobras from human habitations but also conserve the breeeding habitat of the species by working with the Andhra Pradesh Forest Department and other stakeholders.

For the first time in the conservation history of the eastern ghats region, we have been successfully rescuing king cobras from human-dominated landscapes through our snake saviors stationed across the region and also protected a king cobra nest for the very first time in the region with help from the local community.</content>

content.text:
**Unlikely.** King cobra is **not likely to occur inside Elephants by the Lake (EBTL)** as a resident, and even occasional use looks improbable on current evidence.

### Site and method
EBTL is a ~70-acre dry-deciduous restoration site in the Krishnagiri Eastern Ghats foothills, near **Chinnathamandrapalli / Veppanapalli** (~724 m), described by the project as degraded valley forest with remnant wildlife ([ebtl.earth](https://ebtl.earth/)).

I treated “occur inside EBTL” as **resident or regular use of that parcel**, then checked:
1. published range / taxonomy  
2. local herpetofauna surveys  
3. nearby comparable sanctuaries  
4. occurrence databases (GBIF / iNaturalist)  
5. habitat fit for a large snake-eating elapid  

### What the regional evidence shows

| Evidence | Finding | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| **Local surveys** | Ganesh et al. (2018) surveyed Melagiri–Bilgiri–Arcot massifs (incl. Melagiri / Hosur area). Elapids found: *Calliophis melanurus*, *Bungarus caeruleus*, *Naja naja* — **no *Ophiophagus*** ([AJCB PDF](http://www.ajcb.in/journals/full_papers_july_2018/AJCB-Vol7-No1-Ganesh%20et%20al.pdf)). | High |
| **Hosur / Melagiri fauna** | ANCF vertebrate inventory lists spectacled cobra & krait, **not king cobra** ([ancf_melagiris.pdf](http://kans.org.in/sites/default/files/ancf_melagiris.pdf)); Melagiri reptile summaries match that ([Wikipedia: Melagiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melagiri)). | High |
| **Nearest similar habitat** | Koundinya WLS (~60 km; dry deciduous, elephants) lists common cobra/python, **not king cobra** ([AP Forest Dept](https://forests.ap.gov.in/kaundinya.php)). | Medium–high |
| **Occurrence data** | GBIF: **0** *Ophiophagus* records in ~11–14°N, 77–80°E. Nearest wild-looking GBIF points are **~250 km** away in the Western Ghats. iNaturalist hits near Bannerghatta (~67 km) are **captive**. | High |
| **Confirmed Eastern Ghats populations** | Active EG records are mainly **north coastal Andhra / Papikonda** (~600+ km), not southern dry EG Tamil Nadu ([EGWS](https://eghats.org/program/king-cobra-conservation); Balaji & Satyanarayana 2018). | High |
| **Western Ghats species** | *Ophiophagus kaalinga* is **Western Ghats–endemic**; nearest TN rescues are Coimbatore / Nilgiri foothills (~200 km) ([EJT revision](https://europeanjournaloftaxonomy.eu/index.php/ejt/article/view/2681); Coimbatore rescue reports). | High |
| **Habitat at EBTL** | Small, degraded dry-deciduous patch; king cobras need large ranges and high snake prey density. Wikipedia/range texts that say “Eastern Ghats … Tamil Nadu” are **coarse** and not backed by Krishnagiri vouchers. | Medium |

**Best estimate:** roughly **<10%** chance of regular occurrence on the EBTL parcel; **<5%** for a resident/breeding presence. Transient wanderers can’t be ruled out at very low probability, but local absence across multiple surveys makes that a thin tail.

### What would make me trust or reject this

**Would strengthen / confirm the “unlikely” call**
- Continued lack of verified IDs in Krishnagiri / Melagiri / Hosur rescues and surveys  
- No camera-trap or expert-vouchered records within ~50–100 km  
- EBTL remains a small, open, regenerating dry patch without dense contiguous forest  

**Would force me to revise upward (reject the low estimate)**
- A **photo-vouchered** wild king cobra from EBTL, Veppanapalli, Melagiri, or Koundinya, ID’d by a competent herpetologist  
- Forest Department rescue with unambiguous *Ophiophagus* ID in Krishnagiri/Hosur  
- Repeated independent sightings, nest, or roadkill with locality data  
- New systematic survey detecting the species in Cauvery North / Melagiri  

**Caveats:** absence of evidence isn’t proof of absolute absence; surveys miss rare snakes. Still, for this landscape the negative evidence is consistent across surveys, news, databases, and nearest analogous forests — so “likely to occur inside EBTL” is not supported.
